slides.title: Follow a club through a real task
slides.takeaway: Follow Jordan’s club tasks, then Alex’s coordinator review. All records are fictional.
slides.say: Today we are going to follow two people rather than read a list of features. Jordan directs Riverton Pathfinders. Alex is an Area Coordinator. We will see Jordan update the club, prepare a Monthly Record and choose who is going to Fall Camporee. Then we will see how Alex uses those saved records to offer help. Every person, club and event record in these screenshots is fictional. These are teaching examples from the current application, and your own assigned tools may differ.
slides.show: Point to the role labels on the two real application views. Keep the fictional-data label visible throughout the presentation.
slides.objective: Understand the audience, teaching story and fictional nature of the screenshots.

slides.title: Keep the people. Choose the trip.
slides.takeaway: The roster holds club members. A registration selects the people attending one event.
slides.say: The first useful idea is the difference between belonging to the club and going to an event. Morgan appears on Riverton's roster. Jordan can choose Morgan for Fall Camporee without typing the same person again. Jordan still has to decide who is actually going and complete the event's choices. Adding someone to the roster does not register them for every event. Reports, forms and achievements also stay with their own saved records, so we can return to the information instead of asking for another copy.
slides.ask: If Morgan is on the roster but not selected for Fall Camporee, is Morgan registered for the event?
slides.objective: Distinguish club membership from event attendance.

slides.title: One website, several useful starting points
slides.takeaway: Start at events.imsda.org. Browse the calendar, find a club, or open your own account.
slides.say: Everyone can begin at events dot imsda dot org. The homepage brings together the calendar, Find a club, My account and My club. You can look for an upcoming date without opening the director's workspace. When you need your own registrations or club tools, use Sign in on the page. The website chooses the available sign-in route, so you do not need to remember a special director or coordinator login address. A signed-in person may see My account instead.
slides.show: Optional: open Find a club from the homepage. Do not make a new club application for an already-established invited club.
slides.objective: Use the public front door and recognize public versus account tasks.

slides.title: Use the account you already have
slides.takeaway: Use your own email and password. Forgot password? starts the email-code reset process.
slides.say: Jordan already has an account, so Jordan enters the existing email address and password and chooses Sign in. If you received a club invitation, use the account with that same address. If you have forgotten the password, choose Forgot password, request a code and keep this browser open while you check your email. Return here to enter the email code and new password. A passkey may also be offered if one is configured. Making a second account does not restore a missing club assignment.
slides.show: Use a blank password field. Never put a password, usable email code or private registration link in the capture.
slides.objective: Sign in through the current public entry without creating a duplicate account.

slides.title: An invitation connects the account to the club
slides.takeaway: New here? Create and verify your account. Then Accept the invitation for the correct club and role.

callouts.label: Check club and role
callouts.anchor: You're invited to manage a club

slides.say: For a new director, there are two different jobs. Creating and verifying an account confirms the email address. Accepting the invitation connects that account to the club. Create an account only if you do not have one already. Keep the same browser open while checking the emailed six-digit code, then Verify and continue. On the account page, check the club and role beside You're invited to manage a club, then Accept. If the invitation is absent, ask the office to check the address; do not apply to create the established club again. The grey digits in the empty verification box are a placeholder. The real email code must come from the message sent to your own address.
slides.show: The verification field stays empty. The invitation shown is an isolated fictional local fixture, with no reusable token or live link visible.
slides.objective: Separate account creation/email verification from accepting a club assignment.

slides.title: The extra step protects club information
slides.takeaway: Follow the confirmation screen. Use an authenticator, recovery code or offered passkey. Keep codes private.
slides.say: Club and coordinator tools can open information about young people. The extra step helps protect that information if someone learns a password. If setup is needed, choose Set up an authenticator and follow the displayed instructions. Enter Code from your authenticator, then Confirm and turn on. Save the recovery codes privately and choose I've saved these codes. One supported method is enough; a passkey can also meet the requirement when offered. The email-verification code proves your address. The authenticator code is the extra sign-in protection. Neither is an event confirmation code. The grey 123456 in the empty box is a placeholder, not a code to copy from this slide. Use the current code from your own authenticator.
slides.show: Capture the challenge or pre-secret setup introduction only. Do not capture a setup key, QR secret, recovery codes or populated authenticator field. Which app should I use? can be demonstrated separately.
slides.ask: Where does the email-verification code come from? Where does the authenticator code come from?
slides.objective: Explain why a second step appears and which supported choices satisfy it.

slides.title: Open the tools for the job you are doing
slides.takeaway: Jordan opens My club. Alex opens Clubs overview. The tools follow each person’s assigned responsibility.
slides.say: The system shows the tools assigned to the signed-in account. Jordan uses My club, or My clubs if more than one club is assigned. Alex uses Clubs overview on the Area coordinator card; Clubs in the account navigation opens the club list. A person who has both assignments can see both kinds of tools. The coordinator side is not the system administrator dashboard, and it does not give every coordinator editing access to every club. If the expected option is missing, check the signed-in email and ask the office to verify the assignment.
slides.objective: Choose the role-appropriate workspace without inventing a role switcher.

slides.title: Jordan starts with the next task
slides.takeaway: Check the club and year. Home points to the next task and the records behind it.
slides.say: Jordan checks Riverton Pathfinders and the year shown at the top before changing anything. Home is a starting point rather than another form to complete. It brings together the next task, deadlines and summaries, with links such as Open roster and Open Monthly Records. Jordan can go directly to the work that needs attention. A deputy has the director's capabilities; a registrar or reporter may correctly see fewer sections. There is no universal year dropdown to search for on every page.
slides.objective: Orient on the current club Home without introducing a new menu.

slides.title: Add Morgan once, then check the saved row
slides.takeaway: Check for an existing record. Add to roster saves the member; the new row confirms the result.
slides.say: A new member, Morgan Reed, joins Riverton. Jordan first checks that Morgan is not already on the roster, then opens Add to roster. Jordan enters the requested information and saves it with Add to roster. The important part of the second screenshot is the result: Morgan now appears in the saved list. The application also explains that this person can be chosen when the club registers for an event. That is our next use of the record later in the story; it is not automatic event enrollment.
slides.show: Use only the synthetic fixture. Birth-date and age presentation follow the actual account permissions. Do not replace the current row icons with proposed labelled actions.
slides.objective: Add a member and recognize a successful save without creating a duplicate.

slides.title: Correct the existing person
slides.takeaway: Edit and Save correct a record. Deactivate keeps it on file. Remove erases details and cannot be undone.

callouts.label: Save changes or keep history with Deactivate

slides.say: If Morgan's information changes, Jordan uses the person-specific Edit control rather than adding Morgan again. Save corrects the existing record. Deactivate has a different purpose: it keeps the person on file while omitting them from new registrations. Show inactive and Reactivate can bring that person back later. Remove is an erasure action with a warning that the birth date and details cannot be restored. It is not the ordinary way to mark someone absent or temporarily away.
slides.show: Show Edit and Deactivate. If explaining Remove, read the warning and cancel; the teaching story does not need to erase a person.
slides.objective: Choose edit/deactivate appropriately and understand removal is an erasure action.

slides.title: A form can be started, sent or submitted
slides.takeaway: Use an enabled form, then return to Filled forms. Open continues a draft; View and print reads a submission.

callouts.label: Fill in for a member or send a private link
Open a draft · View and print a submission

slides.say: Forms shows the forms the conference has enabled for the club. A director or deputy can fill in for a member from the proper source or use the available private-link process. Jordan returns to Filled forms to see the result. Open continues a draft; View and print opens a submitted form. A sent request is not proof that the person submitted a response. Waiting, expired and submitted states mean different things. We are showing fictional names and state labels rather than personal health answers.
slides.show: Crop away any private URL or access token. Do not send a real request or show member health answers as part of the presentation.
slides.objective: Find form records and distinguish delivery from completion.

slides.title: Capture the October meeting while it is fresh
slides.takeaway: Record the meeting date and counts now. Optional attendance can support the Monthly Record later.
slides.say: It is October in our example, and Jordan records a recent club meeting. From Monthly Records, Jordan opens October and chooses Add meeting note. The date, head counts and short notes are easier to enter while they are fresh. Take attendance is optional for someone who has roster access; a reporter with narrower access should not expect a named attendance list. Saving a meeting note does not by itself submit the month's report. October's current due date is November tenth, so Jordan can keep gathering notes before finishing it.
slides.show: Show the saved October seventeenth example in Edit meeting note. Point to the date, head counts, optional attendance and useful note. Explain that Add meeting note starts the same kind of record; Save is lower in the dialog.
slides.objective: Build a report from timely meeting notes rather than reconstructing the month later.

slides.title: Draft is a stopping point. Submitted is a result.
slides.takeaway: Review the month, then Submit report. Save draft keeps unfinished work; it does not send the report.
slides.say: For this isolated training exercise, Jordan has complete fictional October records and an October report saved as a draft. A draft preserves unfinished work, but it has not been submitted. Jordan reviews the details and uses Submit report, then checks for the submitted result. This demonstrates the controls; it does not establish a policy to submit a real month before its records are complete. October is due November tenth. If meeting notes changed after the report was saved, Refresh from meeting notes is a deliberate action rather than a silent overwrite. September is already closed on our October twenty-first example date, so it is not the report to use for a submission demonstration.
slides.show: Both states must be captures of the same isolated fictional October report before and after submission. Mark this as an exercise with complete fictional records. Do not imply September can still be submitted after its closing date.
slides.ask: Which screenshot proves that the report was submitted?
slides.objective: Submit an open Monthly Record and distinguish draft, submission and a closed month.

slides.title: Choose the people going to Fall Camporee
slides.takeaway: Select actual attendees from the roster. Complete Each person’s details, then continue to Review.
slides.say: Now we use the roster for a different task. Jordan opens Club events and chooses Register or Continue for Fall Camporee. The current steps are Who's going, Each person's details and Review. Jordan selects the people attending, including Morgan if Morgan is going, then completes the location, class or other choices the event asks for. Some choices save automatically as a draft. That helps Jordan continue later, but it does not mean the registration is complete. Read full, waitlist and deadline messages before expecting a place.
slides.objective: Reuse the roster while deliberately choosing event attendance.

slides.title: Review, then return to the saved registration
slides.takeaway: Review, submit, then check the saved registration. Use View to return or download a PDF.
slides.say: The Review page is Jordan's chance to check the people and choices before submitting. The second view is the saved registration, reached again through View in Club events. Jordan checks the status rather than assuming every saved draft is registered. Save changes appears only when the event permits editing. Print club packet or Download registration PDF can provide an authorized working copy. For a church-billed event, the sponsoring church follows the office billing process; this is not a new personal payment obligation for the director. Keep copies within their intended audience.
slides.show: Capture a local fictional event submission only. If a confirmation code is visible, it must belong solely to the isolated demo fixture; no private edit/manage link should appear.
slides.objective: Recognize completed event registration and return to its authoritative record.

slides.title: Turn club records into useful follow-up
slides.takeaway: Record earned honors. Preview an export before downloading only the fields needed for the task.
slides.say: Jordan can record a completed honor through Honors, including Add honors to several members when appropriate. Class tracking handles the supported earned class and award items; it is not a generic checklist for every curriculum requirement. Orders helps prepare supply lists, check stock and track hand-outs. It is not an online store checkout. For a roster file, Jordan uses Build a roster export, checks Preview and downloads the columns needed for the task. These are working copies of the records, so the recipient and fields still matter.
slides.show: If Honors and export cannot both fit legibly, use one large export preview and an optional Honors inset; keep menu references in the spoken notes.
slides.objective: Locate honors and safe working-copy tools without teaching unsupported commerce or curriculum features.

slides.title: Alex finds Riverton and opens a view-only record

screens.label: All clubs · search by club, church or city

slides.takeaway: Search All clubs, then Open. Coordinator oversight usually reads club information; the director maintains it.
slides.say: Now we follow Alex. All clubs is the place to find a known club by its name, church or city. Alex searches for Riverton and chooses Open. The club view says View only and shows the information this role is permitted to read, such as ages instead of full birth dates. Coordinator access does not turn into a director's editing menu. Someone who separately directs their own club can have actual editing authority there, but that is a separate assignment. The current club list contains active clubs; do not expect an enforced my-area filter.
slides.objective: Find a club and recognize the coordinator’s distinct permission boundary.

slides.title: Use Overview to decide where help is needed
slides.takeaway: Check the year, compare the summaries, then open the club behind an item needing attention.
slides.say: Overview helps Alex decide where to look first. Alex checks the year in the heading, then reads the roster counts, reports submitted, total points and last report. Different rows deliberately show different fictional clubs, so we can compare their situations. Sterling Volunteers appears as summary counts; a count by itself does not tell the whole person's story. Alex opens the relevant club before contacting its director. Clicking a summary does not clear the underlying task, and there is no general Send reminder action established by this screen.
slides.objective: Use summary signals to choose a meaningful follow-up rather than treating counts as completed work.

slides.title: Read the status before asking for a report

screens.label: A submitted month · read the saved report

slides.takeaway: Draft is unfinished. Missing is overdue without submission. A points link opens a submitted report.
slides.say: Alex uses Monthly Records to identify a particular club and month. A points value links to a submitted report, which Alex can read rather than asking for another copy. Riverton's September report was submitted October eighth. Another fictional club's overdue September draft and a third club's missing September report show different follow-up situations. Draft means started but not submitted. Due is not the same as Missing: Missing means the due date has passed without submission. A saved draft can still say Draft after the due date. Future months are not yet due, and late submissions are labelled late. In our October twenty-first example, September was due October tenth; October is due November tenth. Read the actual state before asking the director what is missing.
slides.show: Use multiple fictional rows: at least one overdue draft, one missing prior month and one submitted/late month. Do not label October Missing on October21.
slides.ask: Which club has already submitted the month? Which has started but still needs to finish?
slides.objective: Interpret monthly report states and open a submitted record.

slides.title: Explain a total rather than guessing
slides.takeaway: Check the points components. The CSV includes all authorized clubs for the year.
slides.say: The chart gives Alex a quick comparison, and the table explains the same totals. Submitted-report points and yearly registration points are shown separately. The current rule adds fifteen hundred points for an on-time yearly registration. Alex can sort by points or club name. A name search narrows the visible rows, while ranking is based on the full list. Download points CSV includes the whole year's authorized clubs, not just the name search on screen. Check the file before sharing it, especially if you expected one club's record.
slides.objective: Understand points and export scope rather than inferring the file is search-filtered.

slides.title: Club membership is not event participation
slides.takeaway: Read each club’s event status and headcount. Draft, Waitlisted, Cancelled and Registered mean different things.
slides.say: Before Fall Camporee, Alex opens Club events. The useful question is which clubs are participating and how many people are included. The rows show deliberately varied fictional states. Draft is not a completed registration, waitlisted is not a confirmed place, and cancelled is historical. A search can narrow the club rows while the event total continues to describe all registered clubs. Alex uses the specific event state for follow-up; this page does not let every coordinator submit or edit every club's registration.
slides.objective: Review event participation without assuming roster size or draft state is a confirmed registration.

slides.title: Read a new-club application without approving it
slides.takeaway: New clubs is view only for coordinators. A system administrator makes the application decision.
slides.say: Alex can read the fictional Harbor Adventurers application and understand what the applicant supplied. New clubs is a view-only review page for coordinators; a system administrator approves or declines the application. Team approvals is a separate, narrow exception: a coordinator may decide the eligible requests assigned to that coordinator under the event rules. Neither exception gives general editing rights to every club.
slides.show: Point to New clubs, the Harbor Adventurers application and the view-only heading. There is no coordinator approval action on this page. Mention Team approvals only if relevant to the audience; use its own event rules and permitted requests.
slides.ask: Who makes the decision on this new-club application?
slides.objective: Understand the narrow decision exception without implying broad administrative authority.

slides.title: Make the follow-up specific

screens.label: Before · Alex sees October in progress
After · Jordan submits the complete example

slides.takeaway: “Riverton’s October record is in progress. Do you need help preparing it?”
slides.say: This is the practical connection between the two roles. Alex sees Riverton's October draft and asks Jordan a precise question: Riverton's October record is in progress; do you need help preparing it? October is not overdue on October twenty-first. In this exercise Jordan has complete fictional records, reviews the report and submits through the club workspace; Alex can then read that result. The conversation happens through the normal conference process. Opening Overview has not sent an automatic reminder, and Alex has not taken over the director's report. The screenshots represent before and after moments in the same fictional story. An older closed missing month needs follow-up with the director or office; do not promise Alex can reopen it.
slides.show: Mark the two screenshots Before follow-up and After director submission to avoid contradictory state expectations. Any speech bubble is an instructor caption, not an app messaging feature.
slides.objective: Connect oversight to useful human support, with directors retaining ownership of their records.

slides.title: When something is missing, check the account first
slides.takeaway: Check your email. Tell support the club/year, page, action and error. Keep passwords and codes private.
slides.say: If sign-in works but the club or Clubs section is missing, first check the signed-in email. The office can verify the invitation or coordinator assignment. If the password is the problem, use Forgot password instead. If an authenticator is unavailable, use a saved recovery code or configured passkey when offered; ask the office if neither is available. For a page or save problem, give support the club and year, or the event, the page, what you tried and the visible error. Do not include passwords, codes, private links or member health details in a screenshot. The existing quick-start guide can help you describe the exact step.
slides.objective: Describe a useful support request and distinguish access assignment from password failure.

slides.title: Check the result. Sign out. Return to the same place.
slides.takeaway: Try one task for your role. Check its saved state, then Sign out—especially on a shared device.
slides.say: The aim is not to memorize every menu. Use your own account, choose the right club or coordinator view and check the result of the work. A saved draft, a submitted report and an event registration confirmation mean different things. Choose one realistic task to practice next: a director can find the roster or a Monthly Record; a coordinator can find a club and read one month. Then choose Sign out, especially on a shared device. Closing a tab is not the same action. Next time, return to events dot imsda dot org and sign in with the account you already have.
slides.ask: Which one task will you practice first? Use the quick-start handout when you need the steps.
slides.objective: Practice a task, verify the actual result and finish the session safely.
